😎 Happy Sunday! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,563 words ... 6 mins. Thanks to Erica Pandey for orchestrating. Edited by Andrew Pantazi.

🏛️ Situational awareness: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who'd become speaker if Dems flip the House in the midterms, met with Jared Kushner and discussed potential common ground on housing, immigration and the high cost of living, the N.Y. Times' Maggie Haberman and Annie Karni scoop (gift link).
 
 
1 big thing: The "everything's in play" election
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Ten weeks (72 days) from Election Day, the Senate battlefield is sprawling — and stretching deep into Trump country.

  • Why it matters: In a normal year, Republicans wouldn't think twice about Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, Mississippi, Nebraska or Texas. This isn't a normal year, Axios' Hans Nichols and Stef W. Kight report.

Republicans expect all six states to revert to their MAGA mean. But the party isn't betting on it.

  • Democrats have more openings to attack, leaving Republicans with more states to defend.

👂 Here's what we're hearing:

  • Democrats are within striking distance in Iowa, Alaska and Texas. They're longer shots in Mississippi and Kansas. An independent candidate in Nebraska refuses to go away.
  • Democrats' clearest path to 51 starts with holding Michigan and picking up North Carolina and Ohio. Maine is probably next on their list. Then they need just one more.

Driving the news: On Thursday afternoon, the Texas and Iowa Senate races were moved to "toss-up" by Cook Political Report. They were "lean Republican."

  • That makes six GOP seats rated toss-ups or lean Democratic.

👀 The bottom line: At the start of the cycle, Cook Political Report called Democrats' path to a Senate majority "herculean." Last week, Cook's Jessica Taylor declared the battle for the Senate a "toss-up, but one in which Republicans may still hold the slimmest of advantages — especially given Democrats' headache in Michigan."

  • More on each close race.
 
 
2. 🤖 Synthetic everything
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

A shadowy polling firm confessed this past week to faking surveys in two marquee races — then claimed the entire operation was a "short-term social experiment" on misinformation.

  • Why it matters: An AI-enabled flood of synthetic and outright fabricated content is wreaking havoc on reality, poisoning the signals people rely on to understand politics, business and culture, Axios' Neal Rothschild writes.

📊 Catch up quick: Median Strategies, a previously unknown polling outfit with little public footprint, surfaced this summer with two blockbuster surveys that were quickly absorbed into the political conversation.

  • In Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary, Median's fake poll showed democratic socialist Francesca Hong leading Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley by 23 points — reinforcing a broader consensus that cast Hong as the clear favorite. Crowley ultimately won by half of a percentage point.
  • In Los Angeles, Median reported Mayor Karen Bass leading City Council member Nithya Raman by nearly 12 points. Bass cited the poll as evidence her campaign was "gaining momentum," only to delete her post after the survey was exposed as bogus.
  • 21-year-old recent college grad Rahil Prakash revealed himself as the person behind Median's operation in an interview with The Guardian.

💥 The big picture: The cost of deception is plummeting.

  • Robocalls using AI to imitate Joe Biden's voice discouraged thousands of people from voting ahead of the 2024 New Hampshire Democratic primary.

Businesses are also grappling with terrifying new risks.

  • North Korean operatives have built "a secret workforce" inside U.S. companies, using stolen identities, AI tools and U.S.-based facilitators to land remote jobs, according to a Wall Street Journal investigation (gift link).
  • Global consultancy Arup lost more than $25 million after an employee joined a video call with deepfake versions of company executives and followed instructions to transfer money to various bank accounts.

🥶 Not even the weather has been spared: Alabama meteorologist James Spann said he fielded more than a dozen questions about an imaginary late-August "cold wave" this week after AI engagement farms churned out bogus forecasts online.

3. 👀 Flock cameras become midterm flashpoint
 

Photo illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Photo: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images
 

Flock cameras are joining data centers as a top midterm issue, with members of Congress and congressional candidates trying to harness a sudden groundswell of grassroots anger over the AI surveillance tool, Axios' Andrew Solender reports.

  • Why it matters: This blowup over the country's massive network of license plate readers illustrates how rapidly AI has moved from the periphery of national politics to the center of the midterm campaign.

🗳️ Driving the news: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, posted a video on X Wednesday tying his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, to Flock cameras.

  • Ohio Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker said in a statement that her opponent, former House Intelligence Committee chair Mike Turner (R-Ohio), "pushed for more Flock cameras in downtown Dayton."
  • Chaz Molder, the Democratic nominee in Tennessee's 5th District, said of Flock cameras: "That kind of big government overreach has no place in our country or Tennessee."
  • "Politicians are cashing their checks while allowing their cameras to go up everywhere," said William Lawrence, a progressive Democratic House candidate in Michigan.

Between the lines: Flock cameras are emerging as a rare area of bipartisan agreement on Capitol Hill, with conservatives and progressives in particular speaking out in recent weeks.

  • A trio of House Republicans led by Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) introduced a bill last month to prohibit the federal government from purchasing Flock cameras or similar technology.
  • Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) wrote in a social media post Tuesday: "Flock has installed nearly 100,000 cameras across America to track your every movement. ... STOP AI MASS SURVEILLANCE. STOP FLOCK."

The company said it's improving privacy features and told Axios it has been "listening to customers, communities, and civil liberties groups."

4. 🏎️ It's Race Day!
 
Race car driver Josef Newgarden taking a practice run past the U.S. Capitol yesterday. Photo: Alex Brandon/AP

Even for well-traveled IndyCar drivers, today's Freedom 250 Grand Prix track with the U.S. Capitol in the background is awe-inspiring.

  • "We get to race at a lot of cool cities, but this one is by far the best that we've ever had," IndyCar driver Kyle Kirkwood told AP. "Going by the Capitol building, the views here, all the architecture of all the buildings around here, all the museums, it's stuff that you dream of."

The 1.7-mile track includes a lengthy straightaway down Pennsylvania Avenue and another across the National Mall. The Air & Space Museum and National Gallery of Art are both inside the course's perimeter, with a fan zone in between.

Kids walking through the Freedom 250 Grand Prix fan zone yesterday. Photo: Allison Robbert/AP

The Freedom 250 race begins at 1:10 p.m. ET and stretches 250 miles (147 laps) — the second-longest street race in IndyCar history.

  • President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump are expected to take an honorary lap in the Beast before the 25 drivers zoom through Washington's streets in a 180-mph blur.

5. 💼 AI roils the job hunt
 

Illustration: Gabriella Turrisi/Axios
 

Technology has made it easier for people to apply for jobs — and for employers to screen them out, Axios' Josephine Walker reports.

  • AI usage is rampant on both sides: Applicants can automate applications and spray them out, while employers use tech to sort through the flood.

By the numbers: Recruiters process roughly 291 applications per hire, up from about 100 in early 2021, per recruiting firm Ashby.

  • About 63% of U.S. applicants have been interviewed by a bot, while 38% say they've walked away from a job because it included an AI interview.

👻 What we're watching: Ghost jobs, or jobs companies aren't actively trying to fill, make up about 18–22% of posted jobs in a typical quarter, per internal Greenhouse data.

6. 🚁 Fighting fires from above
 
A helicopter battles a wildfire in Simi Valley, Calif., in May. Photo: Hans Gutknecht/L.A. Daily News via Getty Images

Aerial firefighters are responding to this year's busy, unpredictable and deadly wildfire season with more missions, more aircraft and new tech, Axios' Alex Fitzpatrick writes.

  • Fighting fires from above is uniquely dangerous, with pilots flying low over often-rugged terrain and through smoky, low-visibility conditions.

Sam Davis, CEO of aerial firefighting company Bridger Aerospace, tells Axios that several factors contribute to tougher wildfire seasons: hotter temperatures, dry forests with wildfire fuel, and more people moving into wildfire-prone areas.

  • Bridger is developing AI-powered fire modeling tech designed to predict a wildfire's next move, Davis says.

Read on.
 
 
7. 👟 Robots smash human records
 
Photo: Kevin Frayer/Getty Images

In Beijing yesterday, two robots ran faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second world record in the 100-meter sprint, clocking 9.39 seconds. Braking was another matter: The machines slammed into a thick mat after the finish line.

  • The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games, with 2,000+ robots, combines sports with simulated factories, restaurants and offices, Reuters reports.

The intrigue: China makes the majority of the world's humanoid robots. The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny.

Reality check: Humanoid robots can run quicker than the fastest humans. Now comes the real test: Can they handle packaging and warehouse operations, and reliably perform precision tasks like connecting cables — working like humans in less flashy jobs?

Photo: VCG via Getty Images

A humanoid robot plays tennis during the opening ceremony.

Photo: Tingshu Wang/Reuters

One of the robots caught fire after a 100-meter race.

8. 📺 1 for the road: 223 apps, 1 hit
 

Photos: Derek Lacey/Axios, Brock Morgan
 

Brock Morgan applied to 223 jobs over two months before landing one with Fox 54 (WZDX-TV) in Huntsville, Ala., Axios Huntsville's Derek Lacey reports.

  • Morgan — who has a master's from Northwestern and graduated magna cum laude from Howard, where he played football — mostly got the generic response: "Thank you for applying, but unfortunately ... "
  • Late last month, the North Carolina native heard back from Fox 54 about an anchor/reporter position covering sports and news. He starts at the end of September.

"Glory to God!" Morgan posted on LinkedIn.

  • Morgan told Axios: "A big thing I like to tell myself is fish don't jump in the boat."
